title: Bayes' Theorem & Bayesian Reasoning
summary: Deriving and applying Bayes' theorem, the base-rate fallacy, and prior/likelihood/posterior framing — the single most-asked probability topic in interviews.

slides.markdown:
Bayes' theorem falls straight out of the definition of conditional probability. Both `P(A|B)P(B)` and `P(B|A)P(A)` equal the same thing, `P(A∩B)` — so setting them equal and dividing gives:

`P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B)`.

The entire theorem is one line of algebra, but its power is that it lets you **flip the direction of a conditional** — computing `P(A|B)` when you only have data for `P(B|A)`, which is exactly the situation in diagnosis, spam filtering, and any "infer the cause from the evidence" problem.

Bayes' theorem has standard names: `P(A)` **prior** (belief before evidence), `P(B|A)` **likelihood** (evidence's probability if `A` true), `P(A|B)` **posterior** (updated belief), `P(B)` a normalizing constant.

![Prior updated by likelihood into a posterior](assets/bayes-prior-posterior.svg)

The model: **start with a belief, update with evidence, get a new belief** — which can become the next prior.

slides.sectionTitle: The classic medical-test example, worked in full
slides.markdown:
A disease affects 1% of the population. A test is 99% accurate for both true positives and true negatives. You test positive — what's `P(disease | positive)`?

By Bayes': `P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D) / P(+)`. `P(+|D)P(D) = 0.99 × 0.01 = 0.0099`. `P(+)` = true positives + false positives = `0.0099 + (0.01 × 0.99) = 0.0099 + 0.0099 = 0.0198`. So `P(D|+) = 0.0099/0.0198 = 0.5` — only **50%**, not 99%, because the disease is so rare that false positives from the other 99% of the population roughly match the true positives from the 1% who are actually sick.

The **base-rate fallacy** is exactly the mistake the medical-test example catches: intuition anchors on "the test is 99% accurate" and ignores how rare the condition is (the **base rate**, `P(D)`).

The lower the base rate, the more a positive is dominated by false positives from the larger healthy population — a 99%-accurate test on a 1-in-a-million condition still returns *mostly* false positives, since that tiny per-person false-alarm chance, times a huge population, outnumbers the one true case.

slides.sectionTitle: Bayesian updating with multiple pieces of evidence
slides.markdown:
Bayesian updating isn't a one-shot calculation — each new piece of evidence updates the posterior, which then becomes the **prior** for the next update. Testing positive twice in a row (with independent tests) means using the first test's posterior (50% in our example) as the prior for the second test.

Redo the calculation with `P(D) = 0.5` instead of `0.01`: `P(D|+₂) = (0.99×0.5) / (0.99×0.5 + 0.01×0.5) = 0.495/0.5 = 0.99` — a second independent positive result jumps confidence to 99%, since the base rate is no longer working against you the second time around.

**Naive Bayes** applies Bayes' theorem to classification by assuming all features are **conditionally independent** given the class — "naive" since that's almost always technically false (email word choices aren't truly independent), yet it works surprisingly well.

The payoff: instead of needing the joint probability of all features together (huge data to estimate), you multiply each feature's individual likelihood — collapsing an intractable problem into a tractable one. See [naive Bayes classifiers](knn-naive-bayes) for classifier mechanics.

| | Frequentist | Bayesian |
|---|---|---|
| What probability *means* | Long-run frequency over repeated trials | Degree of belief, updatable with evidence |
| Can you assign probability to a fixed, unrepeatable fact (e.g. "this coin, minted once, is fair")? | Awkward — no repeated trials to average over | Naturally — express a prior belief and update it |
| Prior beliefs | Not part of the framework | Central — explicitly stated and updated |

Both are mathematically valid and widely used — frequentist methods dominate classical hypothesis testing ([statistical-inference](statistical-inference)), while Bayesian methods shine when you have real prior information worth encoding.

**Wrong belief:** small `P(evidence|innocent)` means `P(innocent|evidence)` must also be small — treating `P(A|B)` and `P(B|A)` as interchangeable. **Why it's wrong:** these are generally **different numbers**; conflating them (the "prosecutor's fallacy") has caused real wrongful convictions — "1 in a million match this DNA" doesn't directly give "1 in a million chance of innocence," since it ignores how many people were ever considered.

**Correct model:** always run the full Bayes' calculation with an honest prior — this is the medical-test mistake, just in a courtroom.

slides.subTitle: Choosing an informative prior
slides.markdown:
A spam filter sees an email containing the word "free." Historically, `P(free|spam) = 0.3`, `P(free|not spam) = 0.05`, and only `P(spam) = 0.02` of all mail is spam (most mail is legitimate). What's `P(spam|free)`?

`P(free) = 0.3×0.02 + 0.05×0.98 = 0.006 + 0.049 = 0.055`. `P(spam|free) = 0.006/0.055 ≈ 0.109` — about **11%**, even though "free" is 6x more common in spam than legitimate mail. The low prior (spam is rare) again dominates: one suggestive word isn't enough on its own, which is exactly why real spam filters combine many words' likelihood ratios (naive Bayes) rather than trusting any single signal.
